title: Cincinnati
wiki_lead:
Cincinnati (  SIN-sin-AT-ee; colloquially nicknamed Cincy) is the most populous city in Hamilton County, Ohio, United States, and its county seat. It is located along the Ohio River across from its confluence with the Licking River in Kentucky. Cincinnati is the third-most populous city in Ohio (after Columbus and Cleveland), and the 66th-most populous city in the U.S., with a population of 309,317 at the 2020 census. The city serves as the economic and cultural hub of the tri-state Cincinnati metropolitan area, Ohio's most populous metropolitan area and the nation's 30th-largest, at over 2.3 million residents.
Settled in 1788, Cincinnati was among the top 10 U.S. cities by population throughout much of the 19th century. Located at the crossroads of the Northern and Southern United States, the city developed as an inland port for cargo shipping by steamboats; this location also made it a hub of Underground Railroad activity. Although it had fewer immigrants and thus less influence from Europe than major East Coast cities in the same period, it received a significant number of German-speaking immigrants, who founded many of the city's early cultural institutions. Cincinnati later developed a manufacturing industrial economy as railroads displaced river traffic in the 20th century.
Greater Cincinnati has the 28th-largest economy in the U.S. and the fifth-largest in the Midwest, and is home to Fortune 500 companies Kroger, Procter & Gamble, GE Aerospace, Western & Southern, Fifth Third Bank, Cincinnati Financial, Cintas, and American Financial Group. The region's economy encompasses consumer goods, retail, aerospace, financial services, and business services. Its institutions of higher education include the University of Cincinnati and Xavier University. Cincinnati is also the seat of the United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit.
Cincinnati is home to a range of cultural institutions and historic landmarks. Many structures in the urban core have remained intact for 200 years; in the late 19th century, Cincinnati was commonly referred to as the "Paris of America" due mainly to ambitious architectural projects such as Cincinnati Music Hall and the John A. Roebling Suspension Bridge. Other landmarks include the Cincinnati Art Museum, the Cincinnati Museum Center housed within Union Terminal, and the National Underground Railroad Freedom Center. It is also known for Cincinnati chili. The city's major league professional sports teams include the Cincinnati Bengals (NFL), Cincinnati Reds (MLB), and FC Cincinnati (MLS).

grok_lead: Cincinnati is a city in Hamilton County, southwestern Ohio, United States, situated on the northern bank of the Ohio River opposite Covington and Newport, Kentucky. The city was founded in December 1788 by settlers including Mathias Denman, Israel Ludlow, and Colonel Robert Patterson, initially named Losantiville before being renamed in 1790 to honor the Society of the Cincinnati, a fraternal organization of Revolutionary War officers. With a population of 314,915 as of July 2024, Cincinnati ranks as the third-most populous municipality in Ohio and anchors the Cincinnatiâ Northern Kentucky â Southern Indiana metropolitan area, home to over 2.3 million residents. Historically, Cincinnati emerged as the nation's first major boomtown in the early 19th century, leveraging its Ohio River position for steamboat commerce, pork processingâearning it the nickname "Porkopolis"âand, in the late 19th century, "Paris of America" for its architectural and cultural sophisticationâand westward expansion, which fueled rapid population and industrial growth. Cincinnati hosts professional sports franchises defining regional identity, including Major League Baseball's Cincinnati Reds, the oldest continuously operating professional sports team in the United States founded in 1869, and the National Football League's Cincinnati Bengals established in 1968. The city has experienced defining social tensions, including race riots in 2001 and 2020 sparked by police-involved shootings, highlighting persistent challenges in urban governance and community relations amid demographic shifts toward a more diverse population.
